reviewerReport.summary: Independent re-parse of all 110 lines against the source tokens and the ETCSL reference. VERSE TEXT: all 110 lines approved as defensible scholarly renderings of c.5.5.4; zero revise, zero flag-for-human on the i18n.en. LENS-LEAKAGE: zero leaks. Every WoH-distinctive reading (human-creation, brick-mould-as-human-matrix, seed/germination, humans-relieve-divine-toil, Genesis/Atrahasis cross-corpus) is confined to commentary and glossary rationale; not one i18n.en line carries the lens. The human-creation cruxes (L19 'the first of humankind in the brick-mould', L96 'the hoe is what made mankind exist', L20 'his Land began to break up through the soil', L31 'rations for the gods') read as plain renderings identical in force to ETCSL. CLAIM_TYPES: confirmed zero speculative entries, and confirmed no inferred-dressed-as-speculative or contested-dressed-as-direct. The two direct-marked features the task singled out -- the /al/ paronomasia convention and the al(gisal) hoe lexeme -- are correctly direct (explicit features of the source; consensus ETCSL practice). The hand-to-nose idiom and Nunamnir=Enlil are also correctly direct. The seven inferred entries (al-tar split, Uzu-ea/mua, Dur-an-ki/bulug, brick-mould prototype, numun/germination, Ninmena, technical catalogue) are each honestly hedged and rest on named Sumerological scholarship; none is speculative in disguise. WHY AWAITING-HUMAN (not reviewer-approved): every verdict is approve and no entry needs a downgrade, but this is a first populated pass of a brand-new composition whose four lens-bearing inferred readings (Uzu-mua, brick-mould, germination, toil-relief) carry the project's interpretive weight, and two source-damaged/obscure cruxes (L81-82 'sons of the hoe'; L95 damaged sabra/sa-par4 variant) plus the L18/18A manuscript divergence are genuinely insecure in the source itself. These warrant the human reviewer's epistemic-level confirmation and eyeball on the damage. The work is philologically serious and source-honest; a credentialed Sumerologist reading only the i18n.en column would find a defensible translation of c.5.5.4.

i18n.en: Not only did the lord cause what is fitting to come forth,
the lord whose decreed destinies cannot be overturned —
Enlil, who makes the seed of the Land sprout up from the {earth} {alternate manuscript: shrine} —

notes.official: The composition opens by imagining humankind as a *crop*. *numun kalam-ma* — 'the seed (*numun*) of the Land (*kalam*)' — is the human seed-stock of Sumer that Enlil germinates; *kalam* is governed by `kalam-ka-na-ag-the-land-cross-corpus`, and the human-as-seed reading by `numun-kalam-ma-seed-of-the-land-human-germination`. ETCSL renders 'the human seed of the Land'. The Translator's option of spelling out *numun* as 'human seed' in the verse was declined for accuracy: 'the seed of the Land' is closer to the Sumerian and lets the human referent surface from context. The principal witness has the seed sprout *ki-ta* ('from the earth', chthonic emergence); variants have *eš3-ta* ('from the shrine', cultic emergence), preserved via the manuscript-variant convention — the variant shifts the cosmology from soil-germination to temple-emergence. The botanical image (humans sprouting from the ground) recurs at the Uzu-mua toponym (line 6) and the breaking-through-the-soil of line 20; the comparative reach to Genesis 2:7's *ʾāḏām / ʾăḏāmâ* (human named for the ground) is noted at line 6 and kept to the apparatus.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆤 𒆰 𒌧𒈠 𒆠𒋫  𒀊𒋫 𒌓𒁺𒉈  𒇯𒁺𒉈

i18n.en: hastening to part heaven from earth, he set to it,

notes.official: Lines 4-5 are the *separation-of-heaven-and-earth* cosmogony, here as a couplet of perfect chiasmus: 'part heaven from earth' (4) / 'part earth from heaven' (5). The verb *bad* (here *ba9-re6*, 'to open, part') opens the primal mass so the hoe can do its work. The same separation-cosmogony heads Enki and Ninmah (*an ki-bi-ta* — see that overlay's `an-ki-bi-ta-heaven-and-earth-separation-cosmogony`) and *Gilgameš, Enkidu and the Netherworld*; the ANE type is shared with Genesis 1:6-8 (the *rāqîaʿ* dividing the waters). The reading here is the scholarly consensus (Jacobsen, Kramer, Lambert) and is not WoH-distinctive; the couplet simply stages the cosmic ground-clearing that the creation of the hoe (line 8) and of humankind (line 19) will fill.

i18n.en: hastening to part earth from heaven, he set to it.
So that flesh might sprout forth at {Uzu-ea (‘Where Flesh Came Forth’)} {alternate manuscript: Uzu-mua (‘Where Flesh Grew’)},

notes.official: Uzu-ea / Uzu-mua is the cosmic location where humankind first emerges, and the manuscripts name it by its own etymology: *uzu-e3-a* 'Where Flesh Came Forth' (*uzu* 'flesh' + *e3* 'to come out') against *uzu-mu2-a* 'Where Flesh Grew' (*uzu* 'flesh' + *mu2* 'to sprout'). Both agree that *flesh* is the matter humankind issues from; they differ only on the verb of emergence. ETCSL translates the name in running prose and flags it 'the name of a cosmic location'; the WoH translation keeps the toponym transliterated and appends the translated etymology (per `uzu-ea-uzu-mua-where-flesh-came-forth-human-emergence-place`), matching the project's handling of self-glossing Sumerian toponyms and avoiding any lens-loaded over-rendering. In the Nippur cosmographic tradition (Jacobsen, *Treasures of Darkness* 1976, pp. 112-113; Kramer, *Sumerian Mythology*) this is the spot, at or near Dur-an-ki (line 7), where the first humans broke through the ground. Comparatively, the *uzu* ('flesh') substance sits beside the *im* ('clay') of Enki and Ninmah and Atraḫasīs I and the *ʿăp̄ār* ('dust') of Genesis 2:7 — and the Sumerian, like the Hebrew, *names the place/creature for the substance* (Uzu-mua / *ʾăḏāmâ*). The comparison is an *inferred* comparative reading, kept to the apparatus and never asserted in the English text.

i18n.en: at Dur-an-ki he {fixed} {alternate manuscript: raised up} the cosmic bond.

notes.official: Dur-an-ki ('the Bond of Heaven and Earth', *dur* 'bond' + *an* 'heaven' + *ki* 'earth') is the cult-name of Nippur and the cosmological hinge where heaven and earth are tied together (Jacobsen, *Treasures of Darkness* 1976, pp. 100, 121; George, *House Most High* 1993). ETCSL preserves the toponym; the WoH translation does the same and gives the etymology here, not in the verse (per `dur-an-ki-bond-of-heaven-and-earth-bulug-axis`). The object Enlil fixes, *bulug* (token-glossed 'sharp object'), ranges over 'peg / pin / boundary-stake / axis': the line is read as the establishing of the world-axis or world-pole, ETCSL's 'the axis of the world'. The WoH 'the cosmic bond' ties *bulug* lexically to the Dur(-an-ki) 'bond' while keeping the cosmic-axis sense; the peg / stake alternatives are flagged. The principal verb is *la2* ('fix, suspend'); variants have *il2* ('raise up'), preserved via the manuscript-variant convention — the two are not in tension (one suspends the axis, the other raises it).

i18n.en: He set the hoe (al) to work, and daylight broke forth (al-e3).

notes.official: This line launches the defining feature of the hymn: the /al/ paronomasia. *ĝišal* is the noun 'hoe (al)'; *ud al-e3* puns that same syllable into the verb *e3* ('to come forth') so that the daylight 'al-e3' breaks forth as the hoe 'al' is set to work. From here the scribe threads /al/ through scores of unrelated words — verbal prefixes, the noun *al-tar*, the *al ... dug4* 'desire' idiom, and a closing catalogue of *al*-initial nouns. The pun is untranslatable: English sense and Sumerian sound cannot both be carried in the running text. Per `al-paronomasia-hoe-syllable-whole-composition-convention` the WoH translation renders the meaning and appends the Sumerian pun-word in parentheses at each occurrence (the ETCSL convention; Black et al. 2004); the verse text is never distorted to fabricate an English pun. Jeremy Black, *Reading Sumerian Poetry* (1998), pp. 64-71, treats this hymn as the locus-classicus of Sumerian wordplay. On *ud*: the token-gloss allows both 'daylight' and 'storm'; ETCSL reads 'daylight broke forth' (creation-of-day paired with the hoe's first stroke), adopted here, with the day/storm ambiguity of *ud* recurring at lines 36, 47, 59, 62, 81. The hoe lexeme itself is governed by `al-gishal-hoe-mattock-brick-mould-lexeme`.

Then Enlil sang the praise (za3-mi2) of his hoe (al),
his hoe (al) of gold, its head of lapis lazuli,
his hoe (al) whose blade was lashed on with cord, of silver and gold,
his hoe (al), the tip of whose arm was a plough of lapis lazuli,

i18n.en: The lord reckoned up the hoe (al) and decreed (mi-ni-ib-tar-re) its destiny;
upon its head he set a shining crown of earth.

notes.official: *ki-in-du men kug saĝ-ĝa2*: Enlil sets a 'shining crown' (*men kug*, *men* 'diadem') upon the hoe's head. *ki-in-du* (token-glossed '(stretch of) earth') is construed two ways — either qualifying the crown ('a crown *of earth*', the hoe crowned with the very soil it works) or adverbial ('on the tract of earth he set a crown upon its head'). The WoH translation takes the first, 'a shining crown of earth', which reads the hoe as crowned with its own element; ETCSL's English leaves the line partly elliptical (the verse trails off with '……'). The reading is a minor crux of construal, not of cosmology; either way the hoe is being royally invested before it is set to the work of making humankind.

i18n.en: There, {at Uzu-ea (‘Where Flesh Came Forth’) he set this very hoe (al) to work;} {alternate manuscript: at Uzu-mua (‘Where Flesh Grew’), the unassailable,}
so as to settle a head (the first of mankind) at Uzu-mua,

notes.official: Line 18A (preserved by one witness; the {{...}} and variant brackets at line 18 reflect the manuscript divergence and are kept per the convention) supplies the purpose-clause for line 19: *saĝ nu-ĝa2-ĝa2-de3*, 'to settle a head' at Uzu-mua. *saĝ* ('head') is read here as 'the first / foremost (specimen)' of humankind — the prototype individual — the same inceptive sense carried into line 19 and echoed at line 96; see `sag-namluulu-ushub-brick-mould-human-prototype`.

i18n.en: he placed the first of humankind in the brick-mould.

notes.official: The human-creation crux. Enlil places the *saĝ nam-lu2-ulu3* — 'the first of humankind' — into the *u3-šub*, the brick-mould (`sag-namluulu-ushub-brick-mould-human-prototype`). *saĝ* ('head') is construed as 'the first / foremost specimen' (ETCSL 'the first model'; Jacobsen 'the vanguard'), confirmed by the parallel at line 18A and the litany at line 96; *nam-lu2-ulu3* ('humankind') is governed centrally by `nam-lu2-ulu3-sumerian-humankind-cross-corpus`. The *u3-šub* is the open wooden frame in which wet clay is shaped into mud-bricks (Moorey, *Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries* 1994, pp. 304-307): humankind is *cast like a brick*, in the brick-maker's matrix — the image returns outright at line 96, 'the hoe is the brick-mould'. This is a *technological* form of the ANE clay-creation of humankind: Ninmah pinches humans from *im* (abzu-clay) in Enki and Ninmah; Mami / Bēlet-ilī mixes clay with the slain god's blood in Atraḫasīs I (lines 210-230); YHWH-Elohim forms *hā-ʾāḏām* from *ʿăp̄ār min-hā-ʾăḏāmâ* ('dust from the ground') in Genesis 2:7. The Song of the Hoe's distinctive note is the *mould* — humankind moulded, even mass-produced, rather than hand-modelled. This cross-corpus reading is *inferred* (a reasonable comparative reading of shared creation-from-earth motifs), documented here only; the English text reads as a plain scholarly rendering and carries no lens-claim.

i18n.en: Before Enlil, his Land began to break up through the soil.

notes.official: The germination of humankind made literal. *ki ... dar* — the verb *dar* ('to split, break through') — has the Land (*kalam*, the people) breaking up through the ground toward Enlil, the first humans pushing up out of the soil like sprouting plants (`numun-kalam-ma-seed-of-the-land-human-germination`). ETCSL: 'his Land started to break through the soil'. This closes the seed-image opened at line 3 (*numun kalam-ma*, 'the seed of the Land') and the *uzu-mu2-a* 'Where Flesh *Grew*' toponym: the whole creation arc is botanical — seed sown, ground opened by the hoe, crop of humankind erupting. The plant-emergence motif is the Sumerian counterpart to the *plastic* (moulded-from-dust) creation of Genesis 2:7; the comparison is *inferred* and kept to the apparatus. Line 21 (*saĝ gig2-ga*, the 'black-headed people', governed centrally by `sag-gig-ga-black-headed-people-sumerian-self-designation-cross-corpus`) then has Enlil look on the new humankind with favour.

i18n.en: He looked with favour upon his black-headed people.
Now the Anuna gods stepped forward to him,
and laid their hands upon their noses (in obeisance) before him.

notes.official: *šu-bi giri17-ba ... ĝal2*: the Anuna 'place their hands at their noses' — the Mesopotamian hand-to-nose gesture of reverence and submission (`shu-giri-nose-hand-to-nose-obeisance-idiom`). ETCSL renders functionally ('did obeisance to him'), dropping the gesture; the WoH translation keeps the literal body-language and adds a parenthetical gloss. This is a *sibling* idiom of the central prostration entry `giri-ki-su-ub-appa-labanu-prostration-gesture-cross-corpus`, which covers the nose-*to-the-ground* full prostration (Sum. *giri17 ki su-ub*; Akk. *appa labānu*; Heb. *šaḥah ʾappayim ʾarṣah*); the line-23 gesture is the lesser hand-*to-the-nose* salute, the same reverence-family pivoting on the nose (*giri17* / *appu*) as focal body-part. The fuller cross-corpus apparatus lives at the central entry.

i18n.en: With a prayer they soothed Enlil,

lines.translit: uĝ3 saĝ gig2-ga <phr type="VP" lemma="al dug4" label="to desire"> al mu-un-da-be2-ne </phr>

i18n.en: for they were demanding (al ... be2-ne) the black-headed people from him.

notes.official: The verbal idiom *al ... dug4/dug4-ge* ('to desire, demand') threads the hoe-syllable *al* through a verb of *wanting* — one of the most frequent of the puns (recurs at lines 43, 65, 66). Here the Anuna are 'demanding (al ... be2-ne) the black-headed people' from Enlil: the gods want humankind handed over to provide for them. This is the threshold of the *humans-relieve-the-gods'-toil* topos that the next lines (29-31) develop — the same narrative logic that drives Enki and Ninmah (the gods' lament at their labour) and Atraḫasīs I. The Sumerian pun-word is appended per `al-paronomasia-hoe-syllable-whole-composition-convention`; *saĝ gig2-ga* ('black-headed people') is governed centrally.

i18n.en: To give birth to a lady, to give birth to an en-priest, to give birth to a king —
Ninmena set going (al-ĝa2-ĝa2) the begetting of mankind.

notes.official: Ninmena ('Lady of the Crown / Diadem', *nin* 'lady' + *men* 'crown') 'sets going the begetting of mankind' (*tud-tud al-ĝa2-ĝa2*; the verb *ĝar* 'place/establish' carries the /al/ pun) — having just (line 26) given birth to lady, en-priest, and king. The name is preserved as given (proper-name convention). She is identified in the Sumerological literature with the birth-goddess (the Nintur / Ninhursaĝa / Ninmaḫ function) in her *crown-bestowing / king-making* aspect — the *men* in her name tying to the *en* and *lugal* she bears at line 26 and to the 'shining crown' (*men kug*) of line 17; see `ninmena-birth-goddess-epithet-crown-lady`, which cross-references the central cluster `nintur-nintud-ninhursaga-birth-goddess-epithet-cluster-cross-corpus`. The identification is recorded in the overlay rather than added to the central cluster because Ninmena is a localized epithet here; the equation across names is *inferred* (consensus, but an identification rather than an explicit statement of this text). Note that Ninhursaĝa herself appears at line 46 and is governed directly by the central cluster entry.

i18n.en: The leader of heaven and earth, Lord Nunamnir,

notes.official: Nunamnir is a standard by-name of Enlil (`nunamnir-enlil-epithet-leader-of-heaven-and-earth`); the identification is uncontested across the Sumerological literature (Jacobsen; Kramer; Black et al.), especially in Nippur theology where Enlil and Nunamnir alternate freely. Here, as *mas-su* ('leader') of heaven and earth, he names the rightful and precious persons (line 29) and recruits them to provision the gods (lines 30-31). Because Nunamnir = Enlil is a fixed lexicon-level equation, the entry is *direct* (contrast Ninmena at line 27, whose identification with the birth-goddess function is an identification-across-names and so *inferred*). The name is preserved as given and identified in the apparatus; not added to the central triad entry, which fixes on the Enki by-name Nudimmud.

i18n.en: called out the rightful persons, the precious persons,
and those persons he {brought forth} {alternate manuscript: led up} {alternate manuscript: laid out} on a single thread,

lines.cuneiform: 𒊕𒁉 𒄖 𒀸𒀀 𒈬𒌦𒌓𒁺𒉈𒀀  𒈬𒌦𒉈𒇯𒁺𒉈𒀀  𒈬𒌦𒉌𒅁𒂃

i18n.en: and took them up to provide rations for the gods.

notes.official: The humans-feed-the-gods motif. Nunamnir lines the new persons up 'on a single thread' (line 30) and recruits them *šukur2-še3* — to provide the *rations / prebend* (*šukur2*) of the gods. This is the *creation-of-humans-to-relieve-divine-toil* topos: humankind is made to take over the gods' labour and provisioning. The defining Sumerian statement of the topos is Enki and Ninmah (the gods' lament at their toil; Namma's appeal to create a substitute-worker — see that overlay's `kig-sig-line23-substitute-vs-evening-meal-crux`), and its Akkadian form is Atraḫasīs I (the gods complain; humans are fashioned to bear the corvée); the cross-corpus topos is documented centrally at `du-lum-dullu-divine-toil-relieved-by-humans-cross-corpus`. The reading is *inferred* (a reasonable comparative reading), kept to commentary; the *šukur2* 'ration' lexeme is composition-local and not given its own entry, the toil-relief topos being covered centrally. *diĝir* ('the gods') is governed by `digir-sumerian-divine-lexeme-cross-corpus`.

notes.official: The Abzu — Enki's subterranean freshwater domain (`abzu-engur-sumerian-subterranean-deep-cross-corpus`) — is the place 'where the *me* may not be demanded'. *me* (the divine offices / cosmic functions, the flagship untranslatable Sumerian theological keyword) is governed centrally by `me-sumerian-divine-offices-cosmic-functions`, which already lists Enki and Ninmah v 51 and is here extended to the hoe-hymn. The verb is again the *al ... dug4* ('to desire, demand') idiom carrying the /al/ pun (cf. lines 25, 65, 66): the *me* are not to be *demanded* at the Abzu because they are Enki's by right. The next line names the builder as the *al-tar* / Lord Nudimmud.

notes.official: *al-tar* is a lexicalised /al/ pun (*al* 'hoe' + *tar*, which is also the verb 'to cut/decree') that the hymn deploys as a noun in two senses (`al-tar-hoe-wielder-construction-work-pun-lexeme`). Here at line 44 it is read as an agent-noun, 'hoe-wielder', an epithet of Lord Nudimmud (Enki, the fashioner-by-name of the cosmic triad, `an-enlil-nudimmud-cosmic-triad-cross-corpus`) building the Abzu; ETCSL marks this reading uncertain ('hoe wielder (?)'). At lines 45, 47, 48, 54, 55, 57, 58, 60 the same word is the abstract 'construction-work / building-project' (the *gub* 'stand by, assist at' and *ba-an-dug4* 'commission' collocations support the activity-sense). The WoH translation splits the lexeme by context and appends the Sumerian *al-tar* at each occurrence per the paronomasia convention; the claim_type is *inferred* because the line-44 agent-reading is genuinely uncertain and the contextual split is an editorial reading of the syntax.

The mother of the gods, Ninhursaga,
had the mighty (al-tar) light of the lord dwell with her in Kesh,

notes.official: Here *al-tar* is token-glossed as an adjective 'mighty' (a third contextual value of the pun-word, distinct from the agent 'hoe-wielder' of line 44 and the abstract 'construction-work' elsewhere); see `al-tar-hoe-wielder-construction-work-pun-lexeme`. The ETCSL English likewise hedges the adjectival reading ('the mighty (?) light').

i18n.en: and Shul-pa-e, none other, stood by her at the construction-work (al-tar).
The shrine E-ana was made holy by means of the hoe (al).
For the lady of E-ana, the rightful {wild cow} {alternate manuscript: woman} —

notes.official: The lady of the E-ana (Inana's Uruk shrine) is the 'rightful {wild cow (*im-ma-al*)} {variant: woman (*munus*)}'. *immal2* ('wild cow') is a standard bovine epithet for goddesses in Sumerian poetry, evoking maternal strength and fertility; the variant simply has the plain *munus* ('woman'). The WoH translation leads with the principal *immal2* 'wild cow' and preserves *munus* via the manuscript-variant convention. The bovine epithet is left as the source gives it, not softened to 'true cow' (which would blunt the wild/untamed force of *immal2*). Line 50 is syntactically incomplete in the composite (the predicate runs into the surrounding lines); it is rendered as a noun phrase. The epithet is composition-local and not given its own glossary entry.

i18n.en: The hoe (al) deals with ruin-mounds; the hoe (al) deals with the weeds.

notes.official: The logographic *^u2KI.KAL* ('writing for different types of grass / weeds') is preserved in capitals per the source — an unread sign-combination kept in its cuneiform values rather than vocalised, per the project's convention for insecure logograms (see `al-initial-technical-noun-catalogue-vv83-93`). The line pairs *du6* ('ruin-mound') with *KI.KAL* (weeds): the hoe levels mounds and clears growth, anticipating the weed-clearing finale (lines 104-106).

i18n.en: In the city of Zabalam, the hoe (al) is Inana’s workman.
She decreed (mi-ni-ib-tar-re) the destiny of the hoe (al), bringing forth its projecting {beard} {alternate manuscript: tooth} of lapis lazuli.

lines.cuneiform: 𒉆 𒈪𒉌𒅁𒋻𒊑 𒅾  𒅗 𒍝𒆳 𒌓𒁺𒉈

i18n.en: At her construction-work (al-tar), Utu stood by her;
the celebrated construction-work (al-tar) is that of youthful Utu.
The lady of broad understanding, Nisaba,
ordered the survey of E-ana for the construction-work (al-tar),
and laid out, none other, her own E-hamun for the construction-work (al-tar).
The king who reckoned up the hoe (al), who passes his days in its tracks —
the hero Ninurta introduced the construction-work (al-tar) into the rebel land.

notes.official: From line 59 the hymn turns martial: the hoe becomes Ninurta's weapon of conquest. *al-tar* 'construction-work' here shades toward 'the working of the hoe' as an instrument of subjugation, carried into the rebel land (*ki-bal*); the following lines (61-63) extend the /al/ pun through verbs of seizing (*al-ĝa2-ĝa2*, 'brings to hand / strikes down') and roaring (*al-gi4-gi4*). The hoe that builds also subdues — the same dual register the closing litany (lines 99-106) will gather up.

i18n.en: He brings to hand (al-ĝa2-ĝa2) any city that will not submit to its lord.
Toward heaven he roars (al-gi4-gi4) like a storm;
toward earth he strikes down (al-ĝa2-ĝa2) like a dragon.
Shara {sat down} {alternate manuscript: was set} upon Enlil’s knees,
and Enlil granted him whatever he desired (al-dug4-ga-ni):

lines.translit: šita2 ^ĝištukul ti mar-uru5 {^ĝišal} {() <phr type="VP" lemma="al dug4" label="to desire"> al} am3-ma-an-dug4 </phr>

i18n.en: he {mentioned the mace, the weapon, the arrow and quiver, and the hoe (al)} {alternate manuscript: desired (al ... dug4) the mace, the weapon, the arrow and quiver}.
Dumuzid is the one who makes the upper land thrive (al-lum-lum-ma).
Gibil made his hoe (al) lift its head toward heaven;
he had the holy hoe (al) refined with fire.
The Anuna were rejoicing (al-ḫul2-ḫul2-le-de3-eš).
The house of Geshtin-ana resembles the al-gar-sur drumsticks —

notes.official: *al-ĝar-sur* (the *surx* sign given with the complex value UZ3×BALAĜ in the source) is an *al*-initial musical instrument — token-glossed 'drumstick' but elsewhere a stringed/percussion instrument of the gods; the exact organology is debated (Kilmer, *RlA* s.v. *Musik*). The /al/ pun has now reached the temple-music lexicon. The WoH translation transliterates with the source gloss ('the al-gar-sur drumsticks'); the lexeme is recorded in the technical-catalogue entry `al-initial-technical-noun-catalogue-vv83-93`.

i18n.en: the al-gar-sur drumsticks of Mother Geshtin-ana, sweet of sound.
The lord bellowed at his hoe (al) like a bull.
As for the grave: the hoe (al) carries the head down into the earth;

notes.official: Lines 74-75 turn the hoe to death-work: the hoe that brought humankind *up* from the soil now carries the head and corpse *down* into it (*irigal* 'grave / netherworld'; *ad6* 'corpse'). ETCSL reads the paired lines as burial *and* disinterment — the hoe both buries the dead and brings them back up — and notes (in its apparatus to line 75) that this may allude to Enkidu's ghost being raised in *Gilgameš, Enkidu and the Netherworld*, where a hole is opened in the ground so Enkidu's spirit can come up to Gilgameš. The WoH translation renders the down-into-the-ground sense of both hemistichs (the principal reading); the disinterment allusion is noted here. *irigal* ('grave') is rendered with the standard 'grave' rather than 'netherworld'; the occupational/chthonic titles of the hoe in this stretch (74-80) are composition-local metaphors and are not given individual glossary entries.

i18n.en: by the hoe (al) the corpse is carried down into the ground.
As for the mighty youth of An, the younger brother of Nergal —
the hero Gilgamesh: by the hoe (al) he is a hunting-net.
The {(one manuscript adds: sage)} son of Ninsumun is foremost at the oar (ĝisal).

notes.official: Two features. (1) The pun pivots from *ĝišal* ('hoe') to its near-homophone *ĝisal* ('oar') — the son of Ninsumun (Gilgamesh) is 'foremost at the oar', which ETCSL notes may allude to Gilgamesh rowing across the waters of death (the punt-poles episode of *Gilgameš* and the death-waters crossing). The oar/hoe homophony is the same /al/-family wordplay at a finer grain; the gloss 'oar (ĝisal)' keeps it visible. (2) One witness adds *gašam* ('sage / expert craftsman') as an epithet of Gilgamesh — an added word with no primary counterpart, rendered '(one manuscript adds: sage)' per the manuscript-variant convention rather than promoted into the line. Both the added epithet and the oar/hoe pun are preserved exactly as the witnesses transmit them.

i18n.en: By the hoe (al) he is the chief barber of the watercourses.

notes.official: Lines 79-80 cast the hoe in metaphorical *occupational* titles drawn from canal-work and temple-service: *kindagal* ('chief barber / overseer of the watercourses' — the official who keeps the canals trimmed and clear, here the dredging hoe) and *sukkal* ('minister / vizier' of the cella, line 80). The WoH translation keeps the standard renderings ('chief barber of the watercourses', 'minister'); a 'dredger / overseer' paraphrase for *kindagal* was considered but the literal 'chief barber' preserves the canal-trimming image the metaphor turns on. These are composition-local figures and carry no separate glossary entries.

i18n.en: In the {residence} {alternate manuscript: place} of the cella, by the hoe (al) he is the minister.
The evil ones who lie about in the daylight are sons of the hoe (al);

notes.official: An opaque couplet (81-82). *ḫul-ĝal2* ('the evil / malevolent ones') 'who lie about in the daylight' are called 'sons of the hoe', 'born from heaven after sleep had been spoken of' (*u4-sa2 dug4-ga-ta an-ta u3-tud*). The syntax of 'sleep having been spoken' is uncertain and the sense is genuinely obscure; ETCSL smooths to 'born in sleep from heaven'. The WoH translation keeps a literal-as-possible rendering and flags the obscurity here rather than resolving it. *ḫul-ĝal2* ('evil beings') and *u4-sa2 / u3-sa2* ('sleep') are composition-local and uncertain; no glossary entry is asserted for a passage this insecure. This couplet is escalated to the Reviewer in the editor report as an open crux.

i18n.en: born from heaven after sleep had been spoken of.
In heaven there is the al-tirigu bird, the bird of the god;

notes.official: From here the hymn closes with an encyclopedic catalogue of *al*-initial or hoe-adjacent technical nouns, the paronomasia spilling from the verb-system into the lexicon (`al-initial-technical-noun-catalogue-vv83-93`): in heaven the *al-ti-ri2-gu7* bird (83, glossed 'wren?'); on the battlefield the *dur10-al-lub* battle-axe (85); at the wall the *al-lu5-ḫab2* battle-net (86); the *ma-al-tum* bowl (87), *ma-a-a-al-tum* sledge (88), *ar-gibil2* rack (89); on the hill-country the *al-la-nu-um* oak (91), *ar-ga-nu-um* balm (92), *algameš* stone (93). Several are *al*-initial by accident of phonology — which is the point: the scribe is combing the lexicon for the hoe-syllable. The ETCSL token-glosses themselves hedge ('wren?', 'type of net', 'type of bowl', etc.); the WoH translation transliterates each with the best available gloss and flags the identifications as provisional (claim_type *inferred* on the catalogue entry). The eleven lexemes are bundled into one entry because they share a single rendering-decision and none recurs across the corpus.

i18n.en: on earth there is the hoe (al): a dog in the reedbeds, a dragon in the forest.

lines.cuneiform: 𒆠𒂠 𒀀𒀭 𒄑𒄀𒀀 𒌨𒊏 𒌁𒊏 𒃲𒁔𒀀𒀭

i18n.en: On the field of battle there is the dur-allub battle-axe.
By the city wall there is the al-luhab battle-net.
On the offering-table there is the maltum bowl.
In the chariot-shed there is the mayaltum sledge.
In the donkey-stable there is the argibil rack.
The hoe (al) — sweet is its name — is present too on the hill-country:
the tree of the hill-country is the allanum oak;
the fragrance of the hill-country is the arganum balm;
the stone of the hill-country is the algamesh stone.
The hoe (al) makes things thrive (lum-lum-ma); the hoe (al) makes things flourish (lam-lam-ma).
The hoe (al) is good barley; the hoe (al) is {a hunting-net} {alternate manuscript: an overseer […]}.

notes.official: The second hemistich is a *damaged* variant: the principal witness has *sa-par4-am3* ('a hunting-net'); a damaged witness has *šabra-[…]* ('an overseer …'), where the source preserves both the /…\ damage-marker and the […] lacuna. Both the manuscript-variant and the lacuna/damage conventions apply: the WoH translation leads with the principal 'a hunting-net' and renders the partially-readable variant '{alternate manuscript: an overseer […]}', keeping the gap visible rather than reconstructing it. The variant is only partially legible and is flagged in the editor report.

i18n.en: The hoe (al) is the brick-mould; the hoe (al) is what made mankind exist.

notes.official: The hymn's climactic restatement of the human-creation crux of line 19, now as bald identity: *^ĝišal u3-šub-ba* — 'the hoe IS the brick-mould' — and *^ĝišal saĝ ĝal2-la-am3* — 'the hoe is what made the head / the first (of mankind) exist'. The tool that digs, builds, and wages war is here identified outright with the *u3-šub* matrix in which humankind was cast (`sag-namluulu-ushub-brick-mould-human-prototype`; `al-gishal-hoe-mattock-brick-mould-lexeme`). *saĝ* again carries the 'first / foremost specimen' sense (cf. lines 18A, 19). This line is the explicit lexical warrant for reading line 19's *u3-šub* as the human-creation mould rather than a mere building-tool: the hymn itself equates hoe, brick-mould, and the bringing-into-existence of mankind. The cross-corpus clay-creation comparanda (Enki and Ninmah; Atraḫasīs I; Genesis 2:7) are documented at line 19 and held to the apparatus.

i18n.en: The hoe (al) is the strength of young manhood.
The hoe (al) and the carrying-basket are the tools for building cities.

lines.translit: e2 zid al-du3-e gana2 zid al-ĝa2-ĝa2

i18n.en: It builds (al-du3-e) the rightful house; it lays out (al-ĝa2-ĝa2) the rightful field.

lines.cuneiform: 𒂍 𒍣 𒀠𒆕𒂊 𒃷 𒍣 𒀠𒂷𒂷

i18n.en: It is you, hoe, who broaden the rightful field!
As for the field that rebels against its owner,
the field that will not bow its neck to its owner,
the hoe (al) makes that field bend its neck to its owner.
It makes the heads of the vile esparto-grass, the vile esparto-grass, tremble;
it tears them out by their roots and rips away their stalks.
The hoe (al) also brings the hirin-weed to hand (al-ĝa2-ĝa2).
The hoe (al), the implement whose destiny Father Enlil decreed —

notes.official: The doxological close (107-109). The hoe is named one last time as 'the implement whose destiny (*nam ... tar*) Father Enlil decreed' — closing the inclusio with line 16 (Enlil reckoning up the hoe and decreeing its destiny) and the *nam tar* idiom that runs through the hymn (`nam-sumerian-destiny-fate-cross-corpus`). The final line is the *za3-mi2* colophon — 'Nisaba be praised!' — the standard doxological sign-off of Sumerian compositions (governed centrally by `za-mi-doxological-praise-formula-sumerian-cross-corpus`), here naming Nisaba, goddess of scribes and the record-keeper installed back at line 33. The hymn that began by sundering heaven and earth ends by praising the patron of writing.

lines.cuneiform: 𒂊 𒄑 𒉆 𒋻𒊏 𒀀𒀀 𒀭𒂗𒆤𒇲

i18n.en: the celebrated hoe (al) be praised (za3-mi2)!
Nisaba be praised (za3-mi2)!
